posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

In Renaissance Europe, science was being transformed into a practice anyone could participate in and even enjoy. The field of astronomy grew rapidly as new instruments were crafted to make discoveries, as you can see on the August page of our 12,026 Human Era calendar. That is when champions like Tycho Brahe, an eccentric man with a metal nose, achieved notoriety by throwing astronomy parties and collecting great volumes of star data that we still use today.

Villa Yum Kaax is not just a place to stay. Located in the Mayan jungle near Tulum, the villa also hosts weddings, wellness retreats, private celebrations, and other special gatherings.⁠
⁠
Between the jungle setting, rooftop infinity pool, and beautifully designed spaces, it offers a pretty unique setting for bringing people together.⁠
⁠
By: @yum.kaax.tulum

The best travel memories often happen away from the crowded tourist spots. ✨⁠
From hidden trails and small local cafés to unexpected conversations with people along the way, experiencing a destination like a local reveals a side of a place that guidebooks can’t always show.⁠
⁠
🎥: @indirakunwar_

For more than 200 years, Hotel Danieli has been part of Venice’s story.⁠
The building began as Palazzo Dandolo, a historic Venetian palace, before Giuseppe Dal Niel transformed it into a hotel in 1822. ⁠
⁠
Since then, it has welcomed travelers from around the world and become one of the city’s best-known addresses.⁠
⁠
After an extensive restoration, the hotel has now reopened as Hotel Danieli, Venezia, A Four Seasons Hotel, with its historic character preserved alongside new rooms, restaurants,

A piece of Hong Kong history is saying goodbye.⁠
@timmy727 showed us Yuen Wah Bing Sat, a beloved local café that has been serving Hong Kong-style food and drinks since the 1960s and is closing its doors this year.⁠
⁠
Known for its nostalgic atmosphere and traditional flavors, it represents a disappearing part of Hong Kong’s café culture.⁠
⁠
If you want to experience this iconic spot before it’s gone, now is the time.

More than 200 million years ago, a forest stood where Arizona’s desert exists today.⁠
⁠
Over time, fallen trees were buried under layers of sediment, and minerals slowly replaced the wood, preserving them as stone. Today, Petrified Forest National Park protects one of the world’s largest collections of petrified wood, with some pieces still showing the original tree rings and patterns.⁠
⁠
Beyond the ancient forest, the park is also home to colorful badlands, fossil discoveries, ancestral Puebloa

The Australian giant cuttlefish (Sepia apama), known for its incredible ability to change colors, patterns, and even textures.⁠
⁠
Found in Australian waters, these intelligent animals use their mesmerizing displays for communication, camouflage, and attracting mates.⁠
A true underwater masterpiece that looks almost too magical to be real.⁠
⁠
🎥: @jovlogsss

Shima-enaga is easy to recognize by its round body, bright white face, and soft feathers that give it an almost cloud-like appearance. It lives in the forests of Hokkaido, where it travels in small flocks and rarely stays in one place for long.⁠
⁠
Its gentle appearance earned it the nickname "snow fairy," making it a favorite among bird photographers and wildlife lovers alike.⁠
⁠
By: @y.odamon Alan Aprilio⁠

This fruit might look unusual, but it’s definitely worth trying. 🍈⁠
⁠
 Granadilla, an exotic fruit native to South America and especially popular in Peru. With its unique appearance and jelly-like texture, it may seem surprising at first, but it has a sweet and refreshing flavor.⁠
Would you give it a taste? ⁠
⁠
🎥: @twopackstravel

There’s a tiny bookstore in Sokcho, South Korea, where you can buy a book and read it right by the sea.⁠
⁠
3 Feet Bookstore is a blue three-wheeled truck parked beside the beach. Buy a book, and you can borrow a chair or mat, then settle down on the beach and read with the sound of the waves around you. ⁠
⁠
The bookstore only opens during the season for outdoor reading.⁠
⁠
By: @3feet_bookstore

A unique experience in Seville, Spain, where tradition meets sweetness. 🍪✨⁠
A hidden gem where visitors can enjoy delicious cookies made by nuns, following recipes and baking traditions passed down through generations.⁠
⁠
⁠
🎥: @mollysnutrition

There’s an infinite lavender field in Valensole, where rows of purple stretch across the countryside as far as the eye can see.⁠
⁠
The Plateau de Valensole is one of the most famous lavender-growing areas in Provence, covering around 800 square kilometers. When the fields are in bloom, the landscape turns into a sea of purple, with the scent of lavender filling the air.⁠
⁠
Would you visit during lavender season?⁠
⁠
By: @le_sixieme_reve AXP Photography @tang.jan @spring_pix @martysanchezz

Electric eels can produce shocks of up to 860 volts, generated by organs that take up most of their bodies. And despite their name and appearance, they aren’t actually eels. Learn more about electric eels with five surprising facts. ⚡️

Giraffes may have more going for them besides their impressive height. 🦒

In a cognitive test, some giraffes successfully determined which sealed container held the larger total of carrots after more were added. The findings suggest these mammals may have strong numerical abilities that, while difficult to compare directly, could exceed those reported for dogs, horses, and zebrafish in similar studies. Researchers are now exploring what those abilities could reveal about giraffes in the wild.

What are you willing to give up for a longer life? To accompany our September cover story on cutting-edge longevity research, National Geographic commissioned a survey of 1,000 U.S. adults to understand what they really think about growing old. Respondents were directed to select all answers that apply. The results speak for themselves—revealing whether Americans prioritize quality of life over length and if the idea of a society where people live to 150 is really for everyone.

Find out more at

Doctors now have a new way to treat patients with rheumatoid arthritis: an implanted device that uses electricity instead of medication. Designed to stimulate the vagus nerve, the device activates a neural circuit that helps regulate the inflammation behind the disease. It’s a milestone for bioelectronic medicine, and researchers are already testing how targeting the nervous system could change the treatment of other chronic conditions.

Learn more at the link in bio.

Photograph by @balaramahel

A Kermode bear in British Columbia’s Great Bear Rainforest, spotted jellyfish in Southeast Asia's "Coral Triangle," and a blessing of narwhals near Canada's Baffin Island are just some of the many encounters photographer @paulnicklen has captured during his time behind the camera. His new book, Reverence, features wildlife across land and sea while drawing attention to the biodiversity the planet continues to lose. For Nicklen, despite what has been lost, there is still much worth fighting for.
